text:
Keep the Joins: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone proposes that joined-up handwriting should go the way of the slide rule. Children type, the argument runs; adults type; exams will soon be typed; so why spend scarce classroom hours teaching seven-year-olds to loop an f into an l? Finland dropped its cursive requirement in 2016. The American Common Core standards left it out in 2010. The case for abolition sounds modern and practical. I think it is wrong, and that primary schools should carry on teaching children to join their letters. Not because of nostalgia, and not because cursive is magic, but because fluent handwriting is still a working tool of thought, joining is the most reliable route to that fluency, and the cost of teaching it is small compared with the cost of leaving children without it.

Start with what handwriting is for. It is easy to treat it as a presentation skill, a way of making finished work look neat, in which case a keyboard obviously does it better. But in a primary classroom handwriting is the main channel through which children compose. A child writing a story is doing several hard things at once: deciding what to say, holding a sentence in mind, spelling the words, and physically producing the letters. Working memory is limited, and whatever the hand demands is unavailable to the head. Research over several decades, much of it associated with Virginia Berninger and Steve Graham, has found that handwriting fluency in the early years predicts the length and quality of what children write, and that teaching handwriting explicitly improves composition, not just neatness. A child who has to think about how to form each letter writes less, and writes worse, than a child whose hand runs on its own.

So the real question is not whether children should write by hand, since almost nobody proposes abolishing the pencil in Year 1, but whether they should move on from separate printed letters to a joined script. Here the honest position is that the evidence does not show cursive to be cognitively superior to print in some deep way. Claims that joined writing uniquely wires the brain are overstated. The brain-imaging work usually cited, such as Karin James's studies of young children, shows that forming letters by hand engages reading-related networks in a way that typing or tracing does not; it is evidence for handwriting, not for joins.

The case for joining is more mundane, and I think stronger for it. It is about speed and stamina. Printing requires the pen to lift and re-land dozens of times a line, and each landing is a small act of aiming. A joined script lets the word, rather than the letter, become the unit of movement. Studies of writing speed are not unanimous, and the fastest adult writers tend to use a mixed hand, joining some letters and not others. But notice what that mixed hand is: a personal simplification of a joined script. You can only drop joins you have learned. A child taught only to print has no fast gear to shift into, and tends to invent one unaided, usually badly, in the pressure of secondary school. Teaching joins in primary school gives every child the raw material for an efficient adult hand, instead of leaving it to the ones with tidy-minded parents.

There is also a benefit for spelling and for children who struggle. When a word is written as a continuous movement, its spelling is stored partly as a motor pattern: the hand knows how "because" goes. Many specialist teachers of dyslexic pupils favour continuous cursive for exactly this reason, and because joined letters each begin in the same place and flow in the same direction, which reduces the reversals of b and d that plague printers, and makes word boundaries clear. The evidence here is more from practice than from large trials, and I would not rest the whole case on it. But it points the same way as everything else: joining is not decoration applied to writing; it changes how the writing is produced.

Now take the abolitionist's strongest point: adults type. They do. But children are not small office workers, and school is not yet a typed environment. In England, as in most countries, the great majority of public examinations are still written by hand, for hours at a stretch, against the clock. A sixteen-year-old who writes slowly or whose hand cramps after twenty minutes is penalised in every essay subject, however much she knows. Exam boards are moving towards on-screen assessment, but slowly, unevenly, and with real worries about equipment, security and fairness. To stop teaching fluent handwriting now, on the strength of a transition that may take another generation to complete, would be to gamble with the results of the children least able to compensate.

And even in a typed world, the hand keeps its uses. Notes taken by hand in a lecture or meeting cannot be transcribed verbatim, so the writer is forced to select and rephrase. The well-known 2014 study by Mueller and Oppenheimer claiming that longhand note-takers understand more than laptop users has had a mixed record in replication, and I would not lean on it heavily. But one need not believe that paper makes you cleverer to see that it is useful to be able to think on it: to sketch a plan, annotate a text, work a maths problem, draft something away from a screen and its distractions. Mathematics and science remain stubbornly handwritten, because keyboards are poor at equations and diagrams. A person who can write quickly by hand has an extra tool. A person who cannot is dependent on a device being present, charged and permitted.

The second abolitionist argument is opportunity cost. Time spent on joins is time not spent on coding, or typing, or reading. This deserves a straight answer, which is that the time involved is modest. Effective handwriting teaching is a matter of short, frequent sessions, ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week, concentrated in the years from about six to nine. That is not what is crowding out the rest of the curriculum. And the investment pays back in every other subject, because a child who writes fluently gets more out of every lesson in which writing happens, which is most of them. Typing should certainly be taught as well; the two are not rivals. Touch-typing is a skill that older primary children pick up quickly, and there is no reason a school cannot do both. The choice between pen and keyboard is a false one, posed mostly by people who want to cut something.

A third objection is that joined-up writing is taught badly: too early, too rigidly, with fussy lead-in strokes and loops, turning writing into a misery for children whose fine motor control is not ready. This is often true, and it is an argument for teaching it better, not for stopping. Ofsted's research review of English and the Department for Education's own guidance have both warned against forcing joins before children can form individual letters securely. A sensible sequence teaches clear print first, introduces joins once letter formation is automatic, uses a simple script without ornamental flourishes, and accepts that some letters are better left unjoined. Schools that insist on fully continuous cursive from the age of four have given the practice a bad name. Children with dyspraxia or other motor difficulties should be given keyboards without fuss. None of that touches the general case.

Finally, there is the argument I have saved for last because it is the weakest in a seminar and perhaps the strongest in life. Handwriting is the one form of writing that is entirely one's own. A typed page looks the same whoever produced it. A handwritten one carries the person: a grandparent's letter, a note in a lunchbox, a signature. A child who cannot write joined script will also struggle to read it, and so is cut off from the family letters, old postcards and historical documents written in it. American states that dropped cursive have been quietly restoring it, California among them in 2024, partly for this reason. I would not build a curriculum on sentiment, but nor would I pretend that literacy is only about throughput. Reading the handwriting of the people who came before you is part of being literate in your own culture.

The slide rule was dropped because the calculator did everything it did, better. The keyboard does not do everything the pen does. It does not go into every exam hall, it does not draw the diagram, it does not free a six-year-old's mind to think about her story instead of her letters. Until it does, schools should keep teaching children to write a fast, legible, joined hand: start it when they are ready, teach it simply, teach typing alongside it, and stop apologising for it. Fifteen minutes a day for a few years buys a skill that lasts a lifetime. There are few better bargains in the primary timetable.
